title: Dart tutorial: null safety, functions, collections and async — cv.cm
description: Learn Dart from scratch: run Hello, world, variables and types, sound null safety, switch patterns, functions, lists and maps, records, classes and async/await.
answer: Dart is a statically typed, object-oriented language from Google, best known as the language of the Flutter app framework. It has sound null safety, compiles to native code and to JavaScript or WebAssembly, and supports fast hot reload during development. This page walks through setup, types, null safety, control flow, functions, collections, classes, async code and error handling.

sections.h: What Dart is and what it is used for
body: Dart is a client-optimized programming language developed by Google. It is statically typed with type inference, has sound null safety, and compiles both to native machine code (for mobile, desktop and servers) and to JavaScript or WebAssembly (for the web). During development it runs on a virtual machine with hot reload, so changes appear in a running app within seconds.

Most people learn Dart to build apps with Flutter, Google's UI toolkit for Android, iOS, web, Windows, macOS and Linux from one codebase. Dart is also used for command-line tools and backend services.

sections.h: Install Dart and run Hello, world
body: Install the Dart SDK from dart.dev (or install Flutter, which bundles Dart). Every Dart program starts at a top-level `main` function.

body.code:
dart run hello.dart
# Hello, world!
dart compile exe hello.dart   # builds a native executable
dart create my_app            # creates a new console project

body: You can also try every example on this page in DartPad, the browser-based editor at dartpad.dev.
Use `var` to let the compiler infer the type, `final` for a variable that is assigned once, and `const` for a compile-time constant. You can always write the type explicitly instead.

body: On the web, `int` values are represented as JavaScript numbers, so very large integers can lose precision there.

Since Dart 3, all Dart code uses sound null safety. A variable of type `String` can never be null; to allow null, write `String?`. The compiler checks every use, so null errors are caught before the program runs.

body.note: The `!` operator (for example `s!.length`) tells the compiler a value is not null and throws at run time if you are wrong. Prefer a null check or `??`. Also note that `late` moves the check to run time: reading a `late` variable before assigning it throws an error.

body: Dart has the usual `if`, `for`, `while` and `do-while`, plus a `for-in` loop over any iterable. Since Dart 3, `switch` supports pattern matching and can be used as an expression.

Functions are first-class objects. Parameters can be positional, optional positional in `[]`, or named in `{}`. Named parameters are optional unless marked `required`. The arrow syntax `=>` is shorthand for a function that returns one expression.

sections.h: Collections: List, Set, Map and records
body: The core collections are `List` (ordered), `Set` (unique items) and `Map` (key-value pairs). Collection literals support `if`, `for` and the spread operator `...`. Records, added in Dart 3, group several values without declaring a class.

Dart is object-oriented: every value is an object. Classes support constructors with initializing formals (`this.x`), named constructors, getters, mixins and interfaces. Asynchronous code uses `Future` and `Stream` with `async` and `await`, which keeps Flutter apps responsive while waiting for files or the network.

Throw an exception with `throw` and handle it with `try`, `on`, `catch` and `finally`. Use `on SomeType` to catch a specific type. Dart distinguishes `Exception` (an expected problem the program can handle) from `Error` (a bug, such as a failed assertion or a range error) that you normally should not catch.

body.note: Common beginner mistakes: forgetting `await` (you get a `Future` instead of a value); using `dynamic` or leaving types as `Object` and losing compile-time checks; overusing `!` and `late`; confusing `final` (set once) with `const` (known at compile time); and mutating a list while iterating over it.

faq.a: No. Dart is a general-purpose language and can build command-line tools, servers and web apps. Flutter is simply the most popular reason to learn it.

Both modes exist. During development Dart runs on a VM with just-in-time compilation and hot reload; for release it is compiled ahead of time to native machine code, or to JavaScript or WebAssembly for the web.

faq.q: What is the difference between final and const in Dart?
faq.a: A `final` variable is assigned once, possibly at run time. A `const` value must be known at compile time and is deeply immutable, which lets Flutter reuse constant widgets.

faq.q: Is Dart similar to Java or JavaScript?
faq.a: Its C-style syntax and classes feel familiar to Java, C# and JavaScript developers. Unlike JavaScript, Dart is statically typed and has sound null safety.

faq.q: What does the ?? operator do in Dart?
faq.a: `a ?? b` returns `a` if it is not null and otherwise `b`. The related `a ??= b` assigns `b` to `a` only when `a` is null.
